children: It may be tempting to short AI stocks as concerns grow over the sustainability of the technology investment boom, but TS Lombard said investors should not make that trade yet, with another 12–18 months of the U.S. business cycle potentially still ahead.

The firm said many investors believed the AI investment boom was unsustainable but continued buying AI stocks, making the timing of any potential downturn particularly difficult. TS Lombard noted that during the dot-com era, prominent bubble warnings emerged years before the eventual peak, illustrating the risks of trying to short an asset class that continued to rise.

Still, TS Lombard said investors could improve their risk-reward profile by moving away from an all-in bet on AI. The firm recommended rotating some AI exposure, both in the U.S. and internationally, into a broader and more diversified group of global stocks, including the equal-weighted S&P 500.
Such markets could participate in a global growth rebound while remaining less exposed to an AI-driven selloff, TS Lombard said.

The caution reflected growing concerns about the fundamentals behind the AI boom. TS Lombard said capex recycling was still driving 85% of returns in the AI ecosystem, leaving the boom vulnerable to a shift in sentiment. The firm also viewed the coming wave of IPOs as a warning sign, suggesting insiders could be starting to sell their holdings.

Rising interest rates could add another pressure point. TS Lombard said the AI buildout was not immune to tighter monetary policy and warned that the consensus was underestimating the degree of Fed tightening ahead. The firm said higher rates could reduce the expected returns on AI investments and potentially contribute to the bursting of asset-price bubbles.

Debt was another concern. TS Lombard said hyperscalers had increasingly turned to debt markets as their investment ratios reached 100% of earnings, with AI-related tech debt issuance expected to rise from $120B in 2025 to $200B in 2026 and $300B in 2027.
The firm said a deterioration in credit supply could force hyperscalers to scale back their capex plans, with significant implications for semiconductor stocks.

Even so, TS Lombard stopped short of calling for investors to short U.S. megatech stocks, saying the AI theme still had plenty of momentum. Instead, the firm said the risks were becoming more important over a 12–18 month horizon as the contours of the business cycle's endgame came into view.

title: AI boom faces rising risks, but TS Lombard says don't short yet
